Saving, Investment, and the Financial System

ECON 104 · October 6, 2026

Saving and Investment

Saving
  • Saving is the act of deferring consumption.
  • It is reducing consumption today, to consume more in the future.
  • Think about the fisherperson last week, they saved by reducing consumption of fish.
Investment
  • It is the purchase (or creation) of capital, or for maintaining it.
  • This could be for physical capital or investment capital.
ECON 104
02

Time preference

  • Saving is a trade-off between present consumption and future consumption
  • Generally, people prefer to consume more today versus consuming in the future (on the margin).
  • This preference for present consumption over future consumption is called time preference.
  • Would you rather have $10 from me today, or $10 two years from now?
  • Would you rather have $10 today, or $1000 two years from now?
  • Somewhere in between $10 and $1000 to be received two years from now, is your time preference.
ECON 104
03

Why do people save?

Investment
  • Expenditure on improving productivity takes valuable resources.
  • But they allow us to produce more in the future than today.
  • Which also means that people can consume more in the future than today.
  • The stranded person from last week, they were able to increase future production (and consumption) of fish by investing in a spear.
  • Yes, I prefer $10 today to $10 tomorrow.
  • But if tomorrow I can have $12, I might be willing to give up $10 today.
ECON 104
04

Why do people save?

Consumption smoothing
  • People may not earn money when they grow older.
  • But they would still like to consume!
  • Saving allows them to consume in the future, when they do not earn.
ECON 104
05

Why do people borrow?

High time preference
  • Some people are more impatient than others.
To finance big projects/expenditures
  • You want to make an investment, but you don’t have all the required money for it.
  • Or, you might want to buy a house or a car that is expensive
Consumption smoothing
  • People can borrow to spend more money today than they are making.
  • Think about borrowing money to go to college.

The Lifecycle of Saving and Borrowing

The Market for Loanable Funds

ECON 104
08

The interest rate

  • Interest rate is the price of funds.
  • It is the price of borrowing or saving.
  • Savings creates supply of loanable funds
  • Borrowing is the demand for loanable funds
ECON 104
09

Supply of Loanable Funds

  • The higher the interest rate, the greater the quantity saved
  • If I offered you $101 one year from now, in exchange for $100 today, would you accept? (an interest rate of 1%)
  • If I offered you $200 one year from now, in exchange for $100 today, would you accept? (an interest rate of 100%)
  • As the interest rate increases, a greater quantity of loanable funds is supplied (savings increase)
ECON 104
10

Supply of Loanable Funds

ECON 104
11

Demand for Loanable Funds

  • If I lent you $100 today, for you to give me $200 tomorrow, would you borrow? (interest rate of 100%)
  • If I lent you $100 today, for you to give me $101 tomorrow, would you borrow? (interest rate of 1%)
  • Essentially, when the price of borrowing falls, people demand to borrow more! The interest rate is just the price of borrowing.
ECON 104
12

Demand for Loanable Funds

ECON 104
13

Equilibrium in the loanable funds market

At the equilibrium interest rate, quantity of loans (measured in $) supplied is equal to quantity demanded.
ECON 104
14

Equilibrium in the loanable funds market

  • If the interest rate were above the equilibrium level, there would be a savings surplus and lenders would compete by offering lower interest rates.
  • If the interest rate is below the equilibrium level, there would be a savings shortage and borrowers would compete by offering higher interest rates.
  • The equilibrium interest rate is the only stable price for loanable funds.
ECON 104
15

An increase in the supply of loanable funds

Supply shifts right: the equilibrium interest rate falls, and the quantity of loanable funds rises.
ECON 104
16

An increase in the demand for loanable funds

Demand shifts right: the equilibrium interest rate rises, and the quantity of loanable funds rises.
ECON 104
17

A decrease in the supply of loanable funds

Supply shifts left: the equilibrium interest rate rises, and the quantity of loanable funds falls.
ECON 104
18

A decrease in the demand for loanable funds

Demand shifts left: the equilibrium interest rate falls, and the quantity of loanable funds falls.
ECON 104
19

Financial Intermediaries

ECON 104
20

Financial Intermediaries

  • Lowers the costs of connecting savers and borrowers
  • They are like brokers or like used car sales companies.
  • Savers don’t have to specialize in finding borrowers with promising projects – they just invest their money where they’re getting higher interest rates
  • Borrowers don’t have to reach different households one by one to borrow from them
  • They just have to borrow from financial intermediaries at the market interest rates
Photo: Steve Morgan (CC BY-SA 4.0), Wikimedia Commons.
ECON 104
21

Banks!

  • Banks receive funds from savers and pay them interest
  • What they coordinate is the time-preferences and liquidities (how quickly can you convert assets into cash)
  • They then lend those savings to entrepreneurs and investors and earn interest
  • If the bank receives more in interest on its loans than it pays out to savers on their accounts, it earns profit
  • Banks specialize in evaluating the viability of different business proposals so that savers don’t have to
  • This is just more division of labor!
  • Banks spread risk over thousands of lenders and borrowers!
Teller’s booth, Royal Bank of Canada, Truro branch. Public domain, Wikimedia Commons.
ECON 104
22

Bonds

  • Bonds are just IOUs from a company or the government.
  • They are a promise to repay some amount on a specific day.
Image: U.S. Department of the Treasury, specimen $500 Series EE savings bond (public domain), Wikimedia Commons.
ECON 104
23

Stock markets

  • If buying bond makes you a lender, buying a stock makes you a part owner
  • Stock is a small piece of the company
  • Don’t get a claim on fixed interest payments (like with bonds)
  • But you get a claim on a share of the company’s future profits
  • If the company succeeds, the value of your stock could skyrocket
  • If the company fails, the value of your stock could become zero
  • Stocks are riskier than bonds
Photo: Carlos Delgado (CC BY-SA 3.0), Wikimedia Commons.
ECON 104
24

Review

  1. Saving is deferring consumption. Investment is buying (or maintaining) capital.
  2. People save to invest and to smooth consumption. They borrow because they are impatient, to finance big purchases, and to smooth consumption.
  3. The interest rate is the price of funds: saving supplies loanable funds and borrowing demands them.
  4. A higher interest rate means more saving. A lower interest rate means more borrowing.
  5. The equilibrium interest rate balances the two. More supply lowers it, more demand raises it.
  6. Banks, bonds, and stocks connect savers and borrowers. A bond makes you a lender. A stock makes you a part owner.
